## P0: CF Tradeoff 叙事审查 + EE CF 专项分析

检查论文中 CF tradeoff 的讨论是否充分。需要确保以下内容在论文中有清晰表达：

1. **严重度区分**：DR = hard constraint（结构性无效 triple）vs CF = soft preference（individual triples 仍 schema-valid，只是同一实体在不同 triple 中类型不一致）
2. **根因归因**：CF 100% 由 semantic 层引入（grammar_only CF=0.08%），根源是 EVR 模式（>90%）和 type system 语义模糊区
3. **EE CF vs RE CF 差异**：EE CF 15-21% 远高于 RE 的 10-12%。原因：EE argument structure 更复杂（一个 event 可有多个同类 role 的 argument），CF 频率自然更高。如果论文中没有解释这一差异，需要加
4. **70B CF baseline 解释**：70B unconstrained CF=0.07% 不代表真实低 CF，而是因为大量 parse failure/malformed output 不进入 checker。constrained 后 CF=7.01% 是因为 parse rate 提高暴露了更多可检测的 CF
5. **消融证据引用**：确保 grammar_only ablation 数据被引用来证明 CF 是 semantic 层的 artifact

## P1a: 70B DR=0% 显著度升级

70B DocRED constrained: ET/RV/DR 全零（998 docs）。这是所有实验中唯一完全消除 DR 的结果。在 §5 runtime/70B 段落中更显著地突出这一点。不是 overclaim，是数据事实。

9	\paragraph{CF Dual Mechanism.}
10	CF violations arise from two distinct mechanisms:
11	(1)~\emph{Registry override}: the semantic constraint forces a domain-compatible type that conflicts with the entity's previously registered type.
12	The entity appears in multiple relations with different type requirements, and the per-relation mask selects the locally valid type without consulting prior assignments.
13	(2)~\emph{Grammar-first fallback} (\S\ref{sec:interaction}): when the semantic mask conflicts with all grammar-valid tokens, the semantic layer is dropped entirely, allowing the grammar layer to generate any structurally valid type, which may differ from the entity's registered type.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints that enforce structural and type-validity constraints during autoregressive generation:
3	(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar context-free grammar) guaranteeing JSON structural validity and entity/relation vocabulary membership (virtually eliminating entity type and relation vocabulary violations); and
4	(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} that enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
5	%
6	Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations: 15.37\% on SciERC (7 relations) and 18.46\% on DocRED (96 relations), with 1--2\% persisting even after fine-tuning; rates are driven by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology or model scale.
7	Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.20\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp of unconstrained baselines (R-F1 40--46): near-lossless composability at deployment-grade extraction quality.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec.
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql,ugare2024syncode,park2024grammar,beurer-kellner2024domino,jsonschemabench2025} guarantees format validity but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints; type-constrained code generation~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022,scholak2021picard,pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compiles type systems into token-level masks but operates on static type declarations, whereas IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation.
Vocabulary-constrained IE methods~\cite{geng2023gcd,sainz2024gollie,josifoski2022genie,guidex2025,vukovic2024dore,boostcd2025} restrict which tokens can appear but not which type combinations are valid per relation; EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires supervised training and hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
Training-based methods~\cite{paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,lu2022uie,knowcoder_acl2024,li2023codeie,schema_rl2025} provide soft guidance; post-hoc approaches~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} validate outputs after generation.
OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, is training-free, and compiles constraints automatically from ontology schemas.
Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,grammar_aligned_2024,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026,dccd2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.

\subsubsection{Grammar-Semantic Interaction}
\label{sec:interaction}

The final mask is the conjunction of $G(t)$ and $S(t)$, permitting only tokens satisfying both layers (formalized in \S\ref{sec:composition}).
This embodies an \emph{enabling dependency}: semantic lookup requires relation types to be valid members of $\mathcal{R}$, guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
Without grammar enforcement, the model may generate out-of-vocabulary relation types for which no $\sigma(r)$ rules exist.
Empirically, semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) while failing to eliminate vocabulary violations; the full combination achieves 94\% DR reduction.
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (the semantic layer would mask out all grammar-valid tokens), the system falls back to grammar-only control, preserving structural validity at the cost of a potential type violation.
This \emph{grammar-first invariant} reflects a deliberate priority ordering: structural integrity is a hard constraint, while type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Tokenizer-agnostic type masking.}
Each type name $\tau \in \mathcal{E}$ must be mapped to token IDs for logit masking.
A naive approach maps $\tau$ to its first subword token and sets disallowed IDs to $-\infty$, but this fails in two scenarios:
(1)~SentencePiece tokenizers produce context-dependent tokenizations where the same string yields different token IDs depending on preceding context (e.g., after a JSON delimiter), and
(2)~ontologies with prefix-shared type names (e.g., \textsc{Sen}, \textsc{Sid}, \textsc{Side} in WikiEvents) map to the same first token, making single-token disambiguation impossible.
We resolve both with \emph{continuation masking}: at compile time, we scan the full vocabulary to build a prefix map identifying, for each type name, all tokens whose decoded text is a valid prefix.
At decode time, the semantic mask allows any token that continues a partially-generated type name, disambiguating over multiple steps.
This is tokenizer-agnostic, handling byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral) without tokenizer-specific logic.

\paragraph{Tokenizer-agnostic type masking.}
Mapping type names to token IDs is non-trivial: SentencePiece tokenizers produce context-dependent tokenizations, and prefix-shared types (e.g., \textsc{Sen}, \textsc{Sid}, \textsc{Side} in WikiEvents) share first tokens.
We use \emph{continuation masking}: at compile time, a prefix map identifies all tokens whose decoded text is a valid prefix of each type name; at decode time, the mask allows any continuation token, disambiguating over multiple steps.
This handles byte-level BPE (Qwen, Llama) and SentencePiece (Mistral) without tokenizer-specific logic.
